Music has a verification problem. Detection isn't the answer.

A short read on why the industry needs to prove what's human, not chase what isn't.

Read the full research paper →

Jump to: The setup · The analogy · What provenance means · Why this matters · The shift · The economics of authenticity

Section 1

The setup

AI-generated music is already on every major streaming platform. Some of it is labeled. Most isn't. Some is uploaded by the people who made it. Plenty is uploaded by people who didn't, claiming royalties on songs they had no hand in.

The industry's reflex has been to build detectors. Train a model to spot the artifacts of AI generation, scan uploads, flag what looks synthetic, and gatekeep accordingly. It's a reasonable instinct. It's also losing.

Every detector is a snapshot of yesterday's models. The minute a new generator ships, the detector is behind, and the cycle restarts. The cost asymmetry makes it worse: generating a million plausible tracks costs less than reviewing a thousand of them.

Detection doesn't scale. The math has never been on our side.

Section 2

The analogy

Consider a border crossing.

A border agent doesn't try to detect fake passports by examining ink chemistry under a microscope. They check whether the passport was issued by a recognized authority, whether its chip returns a valid signature, whether the document chains back to a system of trust.

The question they ask isn't "does this look fake?" It's "can we verify this is real?"

Music distribution today operates like a border with no passports. Anyone walks up to the gate, claims authorship, and gets waved through. Questions get asked later, if at all, usually after the royalties have already been paid.

Provenance is the passport. It's not a tool for spotting fakes. It's a system for verifying what's real at the point it enters the pipeline, in a way that travels with it forever after.

Detection: chasing what isn't
A circular target with arrows that have missed the mark and a small particle escaping outside the target's radius. Detection is reactive: it tries to catch synthetic content after the fact, and the things that slip through carry no record either way.

Detection
Chasing what isn't

Provenance: verifying what is
A document with text lines, a signature stroke, and a circular seal containing a checkmark in the lower-right corner. Provenance is proactive: the work itself carries proof of human origin from the moment it's made.

Provenance
Verifying what is

Section 3

What provenance means

Four properties define a provenance system worth building.

A signed record at creation. When a human makes a piece of music, the act of creation produces a cryptographic signature tied to that author. Not a metadata field that can be edited. A mathematical proof that the work originated from a verified human at a specific moment.

The signature travels with the song. It moves through the DAW, the distributor, the streaming platform, the royalty collection society, and the rights database. At every step, anyone can verify the chain back to the original author. No central registry. No single gatekeeper. Just math.

Verifiable by anyone, controlled by no one. A label can verify it. A streaming platform can verify it. A listener can verify it from a phone. The system doesn't depend on trusting one company to do the right thing. It depends on cryptography that's been battle-tested for decades.

Unfalsifiable by design. A cryptographic signature either verifies or it doesn't. There's no confidence interval to dispute, no classifier to retrain, no statistical claim to contest. Detection produces probabilities. Provenance produces proofs. The first can be challenged in any royalty dispute. The second cannot.

The primitives already exist. They secure financial transactions, software updates, and government identity systems. The work is bringing them into music in a way the industry can actually adopt.

Section 4

Why this matters

Three groups feel the consequences differently.

For artists. Your work carries proof it's yours, automatically. No filing disputes after the fact, no proving a negative when someone else uploads your song under their name. The chain of custody is in the file itself.

For labels and rights holders. Royalty pipelines stop bleeding to claims that can't be verified. Catalog acquisitions become diligence-friendly. The "unknown writer" line on a black box statement starts getting smaller every quarter instead of bigger.

For listeners. If you care whether what you're hearing was made by a person, you can know. If you don't, nothing changes for you. The system is opt-in for attention, opt-out for ignorance. Both are valid.

The win isn't policing AI out of music. AI is a creative tool now, and that's settled. The win is making sure the humans behind the work get credited and paid for the work they actually did.

Section 5

The shift

The choice is between two questions.

Detection asks: "Is this AI?" The answer gets less reliable every month, and the cost of being wrong sits with the artist who has to prove their own humanity.

Provenance asks: "Is this verifiably human?" The answer doesn't degrade over time, and the cost of being wrong sits with whoever tried to claim authorship they didn't have.

One of these scales. The other doesn't.

The industry will pick. The question is whether it picks deliberately, or by default after a few more years of detection arms-race losses. The technology to do this exists. What's missing is the will to ship it before the loss column gets long enough to matter.

Section 6

The economics of authenticity

The music industry is proving this argument in real time, through expensive mistakes that all point to the same mathematical reality: detection doesn't scale.

The cost structure guarantees failure. Every detection approach faces linear scaling costs while AI generation costs approach zero. More content means more monitoring. Better models mean rebuilding detection. The math never works.

Recent examples illustrate the trap. In April 2026, Taylor Swift filed trademarks for voice recordings and performance photos, incurring exactly the linear protection costs that make traditional approaches unsustainable. Meanwhile, Believe announced "99% reliable" AI detection requiring constant updates as models evolve, expensive infrastructure, and manual platform curation.

Provenance flips the economics entirely. Instead of expensive post-creation detection, implement authentication at source using existing infrastructure. AI platforms sign outputs as AI-generated. Human creators sign work as human-created. Zero marginal cost for creators, mathematical proof for verifiers.

The industry will choose. Either implement provenance before detection costs become prohibitive, or continue the economic death spiral of chasing faster models with more expensive detectors. The Swift filings and Believe announcements suggest the industry is choosing the expensive path. The mathematics suggest they're choosing wrong.
